# Ecclesiastes Chapter 3 -- The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven:

**2** a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to uproot what is planted; **3** a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; **4** a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance; **5** a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; **6** a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away; **7** a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; **8** a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

**9** What gain has the worker from his toil?

**10** I have seen the task that God has given to the children of man to be occupied with. **11** He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, he has put eternity into the human heart, yet so that no one can fathom what God has done from beginning to end.

**12** I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and to do good as long as they live; **13** also that everyone should eat and drink and find enjoyment in all his toil — this is God's gift to man.

**14** I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him.

**15** That which is, already has been; that which is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away.

**16** Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness.

**17** I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.

**18** I said in my heart concerning the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. **19** For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vapor. **20** All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return.

**21** Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?

**22** So I saw that there is nothing better than that a person should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him?

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 3 moves from experiment to theology. The famous "time" poem (vv.1-8) establishes that life's rhythms are beyond human control, then v.11 delivers the book's theological thesis: God has placed eternity in the human heart, yet we cannot comprehend God's full work. This tension — between sensing the eternal and being trapped in the temporal — is what generates the vapor. The chapter's second "enjoyment refrain" (vv.12-13) reaffirms that present joy is God's gift. The comparison of humans and animals (vv.18-21) is not nihilism but epistemic honesty: from observation alone, we cannot prove our destiny differs from theirs.

---

## Disagreement Log

## 3:11 — "eternity" vs. "the world" vs. "obscurity" for ha-olam

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "the-eternity [ha-olam]" | Preserves the Hebrew term with its range of meaning |
| LOGOS | "eternity" | Traditional rendering, captures theological depth |
| PNEUMA | "eternity" | Agrees — the sense of "something beyond" is essential |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** All three converge on "eternity." This is rare unanimity. The alternative reading "ignorance" (from *'alam*, to hide) is noted but rejected — the positive sense of longing for the eternal fits the context of v.11 better.

---

## 3:15 — "God seeks the pursued" vs. "God seeks what has been driven away"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "God seeks the-pursued [et-nirdaf]" | Literal — *nirdaf* is a passive participle |
| LOGOS | "God seeks what has been driven away" | Formal — applies to time or events |
| PNEUMA | "God makes the same things happen over and over" | Interpretive paraphrase of cyclical theme |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted "God seeks what has been driven away" (LOGOS). This preserves the ambiguity of the Hebrew — it could refer to past time, past events, or the oppressed — without collapsing it into a single interpretation as PNEUMA does.

---

## 3:19 — "vapor" vs. "vanity" vs. "fleeting"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "vapor [havel]" | Consistent literal rendering |
| LOGOS | "vanity" | KJV tradition |
| PNEUMA | "fleeting" | Dynamic equivalent |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Retained "vapor" for consistency with the consensus rendering established in chapter 1.

---
*-- SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
